In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is no evidence yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. The default recipe allows only about 32 PPO updates, which is very few. The network also has a structural gap. For each footprint it pools per-cell features (max, min, mean), but it never sees the layer where a brick would land. To judge a placement it must know, for that landing layer, whether every footprint cell is a target cell and whether any missing cells would be sealed underneath. That is a per-layer test that is hard to build from per-column pooling. Round 1 separates the recipe from the network. A uses the baseline network with a recipe giving more updates and more samples (2 epochs, 128 envs). B and C use a new per-layer scoring network: one tests the same new recipe, the other tests 4 epochs with small batches.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev, and training success was also 0. That includes the per-layer network, which should be able to represent the right local rule: land on support, inside the target, without sealing missing cells. Getting no exact builds at all suggests a deeper problem than seed noise or a slightly weaker network. One possibility is too few samples or updates; the most samples any trial got was 231k. The other is that the world does not match the description, as the task warns. For example, the action indexing or footprint layout might not line up with the convolution maps, and then spatially aligned heads would point at the wrong cells. This round tests both. A uses the starting network with 1 PPO epoch, about 426k samples and about 208 updates. B adds a learned dense remapping head to the convolution head. C is a fully dense MLP that makes no layout assumptions. If B or C scores above 0 while A stays at 0, the layout is probably misaligned.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on both seeds, and so did training success. That covers the starting net with 1, 2 and 4 PPO epochs, the per-layer footprint scorer, a dense remap head and a plain MLP. Recipe changes (1 to 4 epochs, 110k to 426k samples) did nothing, so the sample budget is probably not the main problem. The starting net's 1x1 stem works with any channel order, and its 5x5 receptive field can absorb small anchor or footprint offsets. So a total failure points to a non-local mismatch: for example, actions indexed x-major (transposed), footprints swapped, DONE in a different place, or a different reward. Unstructured fixes (the MLP and dense path) learn too slowly. This round hedges with structured, learnable remaps: a head that scores 4 possible layouts and learns which to trust, a transformer that can remap globally, and a learned remap over every action logit. All three also take the legal-action mask as input, since it shows the true action layout.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on the training-success measure, on every seed. That includes the networks built to cope with a remapped action layout: a plain MLP, a transformer, gated layout variants and a learned logit remap. So a wrong action layout is unlikely to be the problem; at this budget the task is simply too hard to learn. Two causes seem likely. First, the shaped reward pays for filling target cells even when a brick also lands outside the target. With gamma 0.95 the +1 bonus for an exact build counts for little, and the agent almost never reaches it. Second, the networks have to work out landing layers from scratch, using very few samples. In this final round I test one stronger inductive bias: per-layer features read relative to each layer, with weights shared across layers so what is learned at one height carries to the others. I pair it with a longer-horizon recipe (gamma 0.99) that gives the exact-build bonus more weight. A cheap starting-network control tests the recipe alone.
